sheet-2.description: The northern end of Midvale, in Wanaque borough, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Ringwood Avenue (Main) runs north and south through the middle of the sheet with house numbers in the 400s and 700s. Fredericks, also lettered Debow Avenue, runs up the left side on a slant and meets Debow Avenue and Stephens Avenue; the cross streets east of Ringwood Avenue are George, 2nd Street and 1st Street, which run to Center and Laura Avenue on the right. The built-up blocks lie east of Ringwood Avenue, where the Midvale M.E. Church (heat by steam, lights electric) stands between 2nd Street and 1st Street, and a smaller group of dwellings is strung along Fredericks on the west. The rest is frame dwellings with sheds and garages on large lots, with a few farm outbuildings, a windmill and an ice house near a pond at the top left. Six- and eight-inch water pipes are drawn in the streets with hydrants and fire alarm boxes, and an eight-inch pipe is marked as running to the reservoir. The left edge is marked No Exposure. A compass rose, the scale bar and the Midvale P.O. lettering are in the open ground at the right and bottom. The sheet adjoins sheet 3 at the bottom, and a small 7 at the top shows that sheet 7 continues north.
notes: Fredericks is lettered Fredericks (Debow Av.) along its length; today's name is Fredericks Street, and the street that crosses Ringwood Avenue at the middle of the sheet, Debow Av., is today's Debow Avenue.
George, Center and the Laura Av. at the bottom are today's George Avenue and Laura Avenue; Center and Laura are probably one street, today's Laura Avenue.
The Ringwood Avenue and Stephens Avenue junction measured 12.6 m from the modern node and was left out of the fit.
The sheet number 7 at the top marks the continuation of Ringwood Avenue on sheet 7.
Midvale, north end: Ringwood Av. (Main), Fredericks, George, Debow, Center, Second, Stephens Av., Laura (Av.), Meadowbrook area; reservoir at top left. 50 ft. Configured by worker.

sheet-3.description: The centre of Midvale, the northern village of Wanaque borough, on Ringwood Avenue (Main) from Stephens Avenue at the top to Belmont Avenue at the bottom. Ringwood Avenue runs straight down the middle of the sheet with house numbers in the 500s and 600s. Furnace Avenue (Road) crosses it near the top, Melrose Avenue meets it from the east at an angle, Pellington runs west to Rhinesmith Avenue, and Laura Avenue runs parallel to Ringwood Avenue on the east from Furnace Avenue to Belmont Avenue. The main street is lined with small commercial buildings among the dwellings: the Union House and the American Hotel near Furnace Avenue, the Midvale post office in a concrete-block row on the west side, a tin shop and stores, a concrete-block auto repair garage, a drug store and the J.O.U.A.M. Hall. The Midvale School, a brick building heated by steam, stands on the west side between Melrose Avenue and Pellington. The rest of the sheet is frame dwellings with sheds and garages on deep lots. A railroad runs down the right edge of the sheet beyond Laura Avenue, and a stream crosses the lower right corner; the area east of the track is blank and refers to sheet 7. Six- and eight-inch water pipes are drawn in the streets with hydrants and fire alarm boxes. The sheet adjoins sheet 2 at the top and sheet 4 at the bottom.
notes: Pellington is today's Pellington Street.
Furnace Avenue is labelled Furnace Av. (R'd), Ringwood Avenue Ringwood Av. (Main).
Melrose Avenue and Belmont Avenue carry their modern names here; in the 1914 atlas the two names were the other way round.

Midvale centre: Ringwood Av. (Main) from Stephens Av. to Belmont Av., Furnace Av., Melrose Av., Pellington, Laura (Av.), Rhinesmith Av. 50 ft. Pilot sheet. Melrose/Belmont carry today's names (1914 had them swapped).

sheet-4-1.description: The southern part of Midvale and the post office boundary with Wanaque, on Ringwood Avenue (Main) from Belmont Avenue at the top to Railroad Avenue near the bottom, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Rhinesmith Avenue runs down the west side, joined to Ringwood Avenue by Cross, Erie Avenue and Railroad Avenue; Laura Avenue runs north and south on the east side at the top. The Midvale Hotel, the Midvale Gospel Assembly and the Community Club (dancing and moving picture hall, heated by steam, lights electric) stand on the west side of Ringwood Avenue; on the east side are a garage for six cars, a taxi service, a fire department headquarters, a row of stores with a drug store, and the Columbia Hotel near the railroad. The New York and Greenwood Lake Division of the Erie Railroad runs down the right side of the sheet, with the Midvale-Wanaque passenger station at the foot of Erie Avenue, and a line of lettering marks the limit of the Midvale post office and the Wanaque post office along Railroad Avenue. Below Railroad Avenue are the Wanaque Post Office and dwellings. Water pipes of six and eight inches, hydrants and a fire alarm box are marked in the streets. The lower right corner is an inset boxed by a heavy line (coal, wood and lumber yard of John Martoccia and Son), which is a separate part and is not covered here.
notes: Cross is today's Cross Street; the other streets carry today's names.
The inset at the lower right (John Martoccia and Son, coal, wood and lumber, block 51) has no junction with a modern street and is not georeferenced.

Midvale/Wanaque: Ringwood Av. (Main) from Belmont Av. to Railroad Av., Rhinesmith Av., Cross, Erie Av., Laura (Av.); inset lower right (J. Martocchia & Son coal and lumber, block 51, Midvale P.O.). 50 ft. Configured by worker.

sheet-5-1.description: The centre of Wanaque village on Ringwood Avenue (Main), which runs down the right side of the sheet from house numbers in the 640s to the 690s. Warsaw Place (Antigo) runs west from Ringwood Avenue and turns north as Warsaw Place (Wausau); Lines Avenue runs west from Ringwood Avenue below it to beyond the Mill road, and Rhinesmith Avenue enters at the top. Along Ringwood Avenue stand stores, a bake shop with an oven and dwellings; west of it, between Warsaw Place and Lines Avenue, are the concrete-block R.C. Church of St. Francis of Assisi with its parochial school and the sisters' house. Block 42 at the top is largely open, with scattered dwellings. Below Lines Avenue the land opens into large lots: the Dutch Reformed Church, heated by steam, stands near the lower right, a row of dwellings and stores lies along a diagonal road at the lower right corner, and the road called Mill runs south past block 61 at the lower left. The Wanaque Aqueduct Dam is lettered along the lower left edge and a wooded hillside runs down the middle of the sheet west of the church. Water pipes of six and eight inches are drawn in the streets with hydrants and fire alarm boxes. The upper left corner of the sheet, boxed off by a heavy line, is a separate inset of the Hercules Woven Label Co. on Ringwood Avenue farther north. The sheet adjoins sheet 4 at the top and sheet 6 at the bottom.
notes: Warsaw Place (Antigo) and Warsaw Place (Wausau) are today's Morningside Place, which keeps the same bend.
Placed from three points (Ringwood Avenue at Morningside Place and at Lines Avenue, and the Morningside Place bend): an exact fit with no spare point; medium confidence.
Mill is not in the modern street data.

Wanaque: Ringwood Av. (Main) at Warsaw Pl. (Antigo/Wausau) = Morningside Place and Lines Av.; St. Francis of Assisi church, Dutch Reformed Church. 50 ft. Part 2 (inset upper left: Ringwood Av. at the Hercules Woven Label Co. and a cemetery, farther north) has no junction: unplaced.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Ringwood Av. (Main) at the Hercules Woven Label Co. and a cemetery, north of Meadowbrook (no street junction drawn; needs the mill or cemetery located on the ground (parcel corners)).

sheet-6-1.description: The south end of Wanaque village at the Wanaque River, most of it the grounds of the North Jersey District Water Supply Commission. Ringwood Avenue (Main) runs down the right side of the sheet, turning south-east to cross the overflow channel and the Wanaque River on a concrete bridge. Highland Avenue runs east from it near the top. The short stretch of Ringwood Avenue north of the river is built up: dwellings, stores, a stone and brick building, a garage and the E. J. Ricker lumber yard with its lumber sheds, building supplies and offices, which reaches back to a railroad along the right edge of the sheet. A siding curves across the upper half of the sheet from the railroad past a storehouse. The Water Supply Commission's ground to the west holds a reservoir basin drawn as a long oval, a brick pump house with its electric pumps, service and repair buildings, an ice house, a shop and buildings marked to be removed, and sites for further buildings; the Wanaque Aqueduct Dam is lettered along the left edge. The overflow channel and the Wanaque River run across the lower part of the sheet. A block of lots on Mill at the top repeats the bottom of sheet 5. The lower left corner, boxed off by a heavy line, holds an inset of Highland Avenue, which is a separate part.
notes: Highland Avenue is taken to be today's Warren Hagstrom Boulevard where it leaves Ringwood Avenue; today's Highland Avenue begins further east.
Placed from the Ringwood Avenue / Warren Hagstrom Boulevard junction and four lot corners on Mill carried from sheet 5; the fit has a scale about 5 percent larger than sheet 5. Low confidence.
The reservoir works of the North Jersey District Water Supply Commission were built in the 1920s; the area has been rebuilt since.

Wanaque river crossing: Ringwood Av. (Main), Highland Av. (= Warren Hagstrom Boulevard), North Jersey District Water Supply Commission works, Wanaque River, overflow channel. 50 ft. Part 1 placed from one junction plus lot corners carried from sheet 5 (low). Part 2 (inset lower left: Highland Av., block 63, Wanaque P.O.) has no junction: unplaced.

Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Highland Av., block 63, Wanaque P.O. (no street junction drawn; which stretch of Highland Avenue / Warren Hagstrom Boulevard it shows is uncertain; needs parcel-corner matching along Warren Hagstrom Boulevard).

sheet-7-1.description: The left strip of sheet 7, on the north side of Midvale, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. It shows Ringwood Avenue (Main) running down the sheet, with Meadowbrook Avenue crossing the bottom. West of Ringwood Avenue only a few scattered houses stand on the open land of block 15; the long blocks east of it, numbered 20 and 25, hold frame dwellings with outbuildings, an auto repair shop and, at the top, a gasoline station and a concrete block building. The strip is bounded on its right side by a heavy line which follows the edge of the railroad corridor that fills the neighbouring strip, with No Exposure marked along it. A scale bar is at the lower left and a compass rose stands at the left, drawn at a different angle from the street. Six-inch water pipes, hydrants and a fire alarm box are marked at Meadowbrook Avenue. The sheet is made of two strips side by side because the railroad cuts the town; this strip is the western one, and the other strip, drawn beside it, shows Mullen Avenue and the east side of the railroad.
notes: Placed from the Ringwood Avenue and Meadowbrook Avenue junction alone, with the atlas scale and the rotation of the neighbouring sheets; low confidence.
Today's Meadowbrook Avenue runs east and west at the same junction; the Ringwood Avenue street name is lettered Ringwood Av. (Main).
Midvale east: two strips divided by a heavy line: left Ringwood Av. at Meadowbrook Av.; right Mullen Av., Prospect, New, Belmont Av. 50 ft. Configured by worker.

sheet-7-2.description: The right strip of sheet 7, east of the railroad, in the north of Midvale, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. The New York and Greenwood Lake Division of the Erie Railroad runs down the left side of the strip with several tracks, bounded on its west by a heavy line. East of the tracks Mullen Avenue runs north and south with house numbers from the 100s to the 130s, crossed at the top by Prospect and at the bottom by Belmont Avenue; New runs north from Prospect near the top right corner. Frame dwellings stand on both sides of Mullen Avenue, with a few outbuildings and two coops, and the blocks are numbered 37, 38, 45, 48 and 49. A stream winds down the right of the strip, flowing south, with an unlettered course. A Midvale P.O. label and an Entire Sheet note are at the top right, and a north arrow stands at the centre. Six-inch water pipes and hydrants are marked in the streets, and the lower left holds a No Exposure note along the track. The edges of the strip are open ground and the area to the left belongs to the neighbouring strip of the same sheet.
notes: Prospect and New are today's Prospect Street and New Street.
Placed from three junctions (Mullen Avenue and Prospect Street, New Street and Prospect Street, Mullen Avenue and Belmont Avenue), so the fit is exact and has no leave-one-out check; low confidence.
The north arrow on this strip points straight up, which does not agree with the north fitted from the streets.
Midvale east: two strips divided by a heavy line: left Ringwood Av. at Meadowbrook Av.; right Mullen Av., Prospect, New, Belmont Av. 50 ft. Configured by worker.

sheet-8-1.description: The left strip of sheet 8, on the north side of Haskell, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. Ringwood Avenue (Main) runs down the strip, with Orchard running west from it about two thirds of the way down and Maple Avenue crossing it near the bottom; a second Maple Av. runs east from Ringwood Avenue to the heavy line on the strip's right. The land is open, with scattered frame dwellings on both sides of Ringwood Avenue, a garage for six cars (heated by stove, lights electric, cement floor) on the west side, a few barns, and a building drawn with a crossed box at the left edge. The blocks are numbered 66, 68, 69 and 105. The Wanaque River comes in at the top, runs down to the heavy line on the right and is shown with its bank, and a heavy line follows the railroad corridor between this strip and the next, with No Exposure marked beside it. A north arrow stands at the centre and the scale bar is at the lower left, with A-B match line lettering at the top and bottom. Six- and eight-inch water pipes and hydrants are marked on Ringwood Avenue.
notes: Orchard is today's Orchard Street and Maple Av. is today's Maple Avenue.
Placed from the Orchard and Ringwood Avenue junction alone with the scale of the neighbouring strip; the Maple Avenue junction lies 5.8 m from the fit, so the fit is low confidence.
The three strips of this sheet show successive stretches of Ringwood Avenue, north to south from left to right.

Haskell north: three strips of Ringwood Av. (Main) divided by heavy lines: left with Orchard, Maple Av., Storms Av.; middle with Jenkins Av., Smith Av.; right with Burnside Pl., Haskell School. 50 ft. Configured by worker.

sheet-8-2.description: The middle strip of sheet 8, in Haskell, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. It is bounded on the left by a heavy line along the railroad corridor and on the right by a second heavy line, with No Exposure marked along both. Ringwood Avenue (Main) runs down the strip with house numbers in the 900s. Jenkins crosses it near the top and Smith runs east from it just below, and Storms Avenue crosses it near the bottom. Frame dwellings stand along both sides of Ringwood Avenue, with a gasoline station and an auto repair shop north of Smith, and a few sheds and outbuildings west of the avenue. The blocks are numbered 69, 70, 76, 104, 105 and 106. A compass rose stands at the top right of the strip and the lines A-B and C-D, the match lines for the adjoining sheets, are lettered at the top and bottom edges. A fire alarm box and six- and eight-inch water pipes with hydrants are marked in the streets. The strip lies between the strip drawn on its left, which shows the northern part of the avenue, and the one on its right, which is Du Pont's Haskell village.
notes: Jenkins Av., Smith Av. and Storms Av. are today's Jenkins Avenue, Smith Avenue and Storms Avenue.
All three junctions used lie along Ringwood Avenue, so the fit is a helmert placement; low confidence.

Haskell north: three strips of Ringwood Av. (Main) divided by heavy lines: left with Orchard, Maple Av., Storms Av.; middle with Jenkins Av., Smith Av.; right with Burnside Pl., Haskell School. 50 ft. Configured by worker.

sheet-8-3.description: The right strip of sheet 8, the Du Pont village at Haskell, drawn at 50 feet to an inch. A heavy line bounds it on the left. Ringwood Avenue (Main) runs down the strip with Burnside Pl. crossing it about two fifths of the way down, with the rows of company dwellings of the Du Pont village beyond. At the top stands the Haskell School (heated by steam, lights electric), a large brick building, with a frame building beside it. Down the east side of the avenue the dwellings are lettered as owned by E. I. Du Pont De Nemours Co. and as private dwellings with hose, and a note to the right says Dupont Village Beyond. The land west of the avenue and between it and the heavy line is open, with blocks numbered 76, 105, 106 and 67. A Haskell P.O. label with an Entire Sheet note is at the top right. Six- and eight-inch water pipes with hydrants are marked along Ringwood Avenue, and a No Exposure note runs along the bottom and the heavy line.
notes: Burnside Pl. is today's Burnside Place.
Placed from the Ringwood Avenue and Burnside Place junction alone, with the scale of the neighbouring strip and its rotation; low confidence.

Haskell north: three strips of Ringwood Av. (Main) divided by heavy lines: left with Orchard, Maple Av., Storms Av.; middle with Jenkins Av., Smith Av.; right with Burnside Pl., Haskell School. 50 ft. Configured by worker.

sheet-9-1.description: The left of two side-by-side strips on sheet 9, showing the business centre of Haskell on Ringwood Avenue (Main) from Doty Road to below Pierce Avenue. Ringwood Avenue runs down the middle of the strip with house numbers from about 125 to 188; Doty Road crosses the top at an angle, Pierce Avenue runs west at about two thirds of the way down, and Brook runs down the left edge between them. At the top, on Ringwood Avenue and Doty Road, stand the Haskell Hotel, a stone building with a garage and club, a tin shop and stores, a concrete-block store and the post office; a switch from the Erie Railroad to the powder mill crosses the top of the strip. The west side of Ringwood Avenue between Doty Road and Pierce Avenue is lined with stores and dwellings, several in concrete block. South of Pierce Avenue the Western Leather & Sheep Lined Coat Co. has a concrete-block factory with power and lights by electricity. The east side of Ringwood Avenue is block 79, largely open ground belonging to the Du Pont Co., with a dwelling house and hose station, and a road leads south-east from the bottom of the strip. A compass rose stands at the right edge of the strip. The top left corner, boxed off by a heavy line, holds a small separate inset of Ridgewood Avenue (Main), and the strip is divided from the right one by a heavy vertical line.
notes: Brook is today's Brook Street.
The Doty Road junction is today's three-way node of Doty Road, Ringwood Avenue and 2nd Avenue.
Placed from four junctions (Doty Road and Pierce Avenue at Ringwood Avenue and at Brook); fitted scale about 3 percent smaller than sheet 3.

Haskell centre: two strips divided by a heavy line plus a small inset at top left. Part 1 left strip Ringwood Av. (Main) with Doty R'd, Pierce Av., Brook; part 2 inset (Ridgewood Av. (Main), block 76, switch to powder mill) unplaced; part 3 right strip Ringwood Av. from Coles Av. to Whistler Pl., Richmond Pl. (= Franklin Place). 50 ft.
Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Ridgewood Av. (Main), block 76, switch to powder mill (small corner inset with no junction; needs carried points from a placed neighbour drawing block 76).

sheet-9-3.description: The right of two side-by-side strips on sheet 9, continuing Ringwood Avenue (Main) south through Haskell from Coles Avenue to Whistler Place. Ringwood Avenue runs down the strip with house numbers from about 100 to 162. Coles Avenue runs west from it near the top, and Whistler Place runs east from it near the bottom, where Richmond Place leaves Whistler Place to the south. The west side of Ringwood Avenue near Coles Avenue is lined with stores and dwellings; the east side, opposite, has a row of stores with a tin shop and dwellings, followed by more dwellings with sheds and garages. Further south the frontage thins out to scattered houses. A gasoline station with its pumps stands on the west side above Whistler Place, and a dwelling house and hose station of the Du Pont Co. is at the corner of Whistler Place. Along the right edge the strip is labelled as the E. I. du Pont de Nemours company's lower village, beyond the drawn frontage. The large figure 10 at the bottom refers the area below Whistler Place to sheet 10. The scale bar, 50 feet to an inch, is drawn at the bottom of the strip.
notes: Richmond Place is taken to be today's Franklin Place, which leaves Whistler Place 55 m east of Ringwood Avenue and runs the same way.
Placed from three junctions (Coles Avenue and Whistler Place at Ringwood Avenue, Franklin Place at Whistler Place): an exact fit with no spare point; medium confidence.

Haskell centre: two strips divided by a heavy line plus a small inset at top left. Part 1 left strip Ringwood Av. (Main) with Doty R'd, Pierce Av., Brook; part 2 inset (Ridgewood Av. (Main), block 76, switch to powder mill) unplaced; part 3 right strip Ringwood Av. from Coles Av. to Whistler Pl., Richmond Pl. (= Franklin Place). 50 ft.
Not georeferenced on this sheet: inset: Ridgewood Av. (Main), block 76, switch to powder mill (small corner inset with no junction; needs carried points from a placed neighbour drawing block 76).

sheet-10-1.description: The southern end of Haskell, drawn at 100 feet to an inch on a paper that scanned pinker than the other sheets. It runs from Whistler Place and the Du Pont village at the top to Bloomingdale Road or Butler Avenue at the bottom. Ringwood Avenue (Main) runs down the right half of the sheet, with house numbers from about 200 to 283. Haskell Avenue and Greenwood Avenue run parallel to it further west, joined to it by 1st Avenue at the top and by Bloomingdale Road or Butler Avenue at the bottom. 4th Avenue (Mullen Avenue) runs east from Haskell Avenue, which jogs just south of it. Between Haskell Avenue and Ringwood Avenue a brook winds south through a swamp, crossed by 1st Avenue and Butler Avenue on small bridges. The Greenwood Lake Division of the Erie Railroad runs down the sheet between Greenwood Avenue and Haskell Avenue, with sidings at the top for the Phil Fuels Co. yard, whose fuel oil tanks, pump house and office are drawn north of 1st Avenue. The houses are almost all frame dwellings with sheds and garages, spread thinly along the streets; a private bakery and a private oven stand off Greenwood Avenue. At the top right, Richmond Place and Aspinwall Place are the streets of the E. I. Du Pont De N. Co. Lower Village, a row of two-storey company dwellings with private hydrants. The land west of Greenwood Avenue is marked vacant and hillside, and the right edge is wooded hillside with the powder works beyond. A compass rose stands at the upper left. The lower right corner holds an inset at Doty Road, which is a separate part.
notes: Bloomingdale Road or Butler Avenue is today's Union Avenue; 4th Avenue (Mullen Avenue) is at today's Mann Place.
Ringwood Avenue is labelled Ringwood Av. (Main).

Drawn loosely: the two Haskell Avenue junctions at 1st Avenue and 4th Avenue disagree by 6 to 9 m with a fit to the other points and were left out; the part is placed from Union Avenue, Ringwood Avenue and Whistler Place.
The compass rose points about 12 degrees clockwise of the north given by the streets.
Richmond Place and Aspinwall Place were streets of the Du Pont company village and were not matched to modern names.

Haskell south at 100 ft to an inch: Ringwood Av. (Main), Whistler Pl., 1st Av., Haskell Av., Greenwood Av., 4th Av. sheet-10-2.description: An inset in the lower right corner of sheet 10, boxed by a heavy line, showing Doty Road where it crosses the Greenwood Lake Division of the Erie Railroad and meets Brook, in Haskell. It is drawn at about the same scale as the main sheet but turned roughly ten degrees from it, with its own north arrow. Lake Washington fills the upper left of the inset, its shore running down to Doty Road, which carries a six-inch water pipe. The railroad crosses Doty Road just east of the lake; beside the track stand the Haskell passenger station and a freight house. South of Doty Road and east of the railroad is a concrete-block garage with electric light and power. Brook, a street 30 feet wide, runs south from Doty Road with a water pipe, and a dwelling with a garage stands at the corner east of it. The large block number 9 refers the area to sheet 9, and the blocks are numbered 76 and 77. The inset is placed from the Doty Road and Brook junction alone, with the scale of the main sheet and the rotation measured from the two streets.
notes: Brook (lettered BROOK on the inset) is today's Brook Street.
The Haskell passenger station and freight house of the Erie Greenwood Lake Division stood here; the line is abandoned.
Placed from one point (Doty Road / Brook) with the main sheet's scale and the rotation of the drawn streets; low confidence.
